proposals.new_text:
---
title: "Why checking your bank balance feels worse than just not knowing"
pubDate: "2026-09-14"
description: "The avoidance isn't laziness. It's a protection mechanism. Here's what it's actually protecting you from."
tags: ["money avoidance", "behavioural economics", "self-awareness"]
author: "Joel"
status: "ready"
---

Somewhere around the time Joel was earning good money and still hadn't opened his tax-return tab for six weeks, he noticed something. The not-looking didn't feel like laziness. It felt like relief.

That distinction matters.

If you avoid checking your balance, you're probably not disorganised. You're probably doing something quite specific: you're protecting a version of yourself that hasn't failed yet. The moment you look, the number is real. And a real number means you have to respond to it.

Behavioural economists call part of this "ostrich effect" — the measurable tendency to check financial accounts less often when markets fall or spending has gone up. It isn't irrational in the way people mean when they call something irrational. It's a completely logical response to anticipated pain.

The problem is that the protection has a cost. Every day the tab stays closed, the number is still moving. The balance doesn't pause while you feel ready.

What tends to help isn't motivation. It isn't a budgeting app, or a Sunday planning session with a nice notebook. What tends to help is getting honest about what you think the number will mean about you — not what it will mean for your finances, but what story you've already written about what a bad number says about who you are.

That story is usually older than the current balance. It usually predates the job, the salary, the account. It's worth finding out what it actually says.
